pages.text:
After conducting research into autopilot software commonly used by professionals and
hobbyists, three autopilot software options were evaluated: ArduPilot, PX4, and a homemade
Python-based navigation algorithm. The Python algorithm option was quickly eliminated due to the
significant time required to build navigation, control, and failsafe functions from scratch. The trade
study therefore focused on ArduPilot and PX4, both of which are fully developed, open-source, nocost systems supported by our selected hardware. While each offers sufficient autonomy features
and hardware compatibility, ArduPilot provides a larger documentation base and community support
network, reducing integration risk and easing development. This comes at the cost of PX4 having
higher customizability and popularity in commercial markets; however, these were both deemed
insignificant factors in our case. For these reasons, ArduPilot was selected as the primary navigation
software. However, because the hardware fully supports both platforms, switching to PX4 was a loweffort fallback option if the project needed a change.

1.2 Hull Designs
Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USV), or drone boats, have been in development since the early
1900s for autonomous military and oceanographic applications. ASNE has hosted the PEP
competition to promote naval engineering since 2018, providing a wealth of information on past
competitors and successful designs.
A basic design consideration is inboard versus outboard motors. Inboard motors keep the
motor inside the hull, translating power via driveshaft to a propeller. Outboard motor systems are
mounted externally and can be submerged. This choice affects hydrodynamic drag and efficiency,
center of gravity, and speed. Thermal performance is also considered. Outboard motors have the
benefit of being cooled by the environment, namely cold water. This would decrease the need for a
separate cooling system for the motors. Inboard motors are housed inside the hull and therefore are
not passively cooled. This could result in thermal complications and may require a cooling system.
Steering strategy is another important factor for race completion. Responsive and accurate
maneuvering capabilities at high speeds guarantee reliability and repeatability on the course.
Differential steering and rudder control are the two approaches considered. Differential steering
updates thruster power to change the angle of the thrust vector, effectively turning the USV. No
additional mechanisms are required. Differential steering requires a robust control system to provide
fast responses and tight turning angles. Rudder control adds a control surface to the aft of the
vehicle that generates lateral lift, affecting the yaw angle of the USV. This approach is efficient at
high speeds and allows both motors to operate at optimal power. However, rudder control adds
mechanical complexity and drag.
After considering all trades, our team decided on a trimaran design with outboard differential
motors. This provides an optimal balance of speed, control, and efficiency suitable for our goals.

1.3 Controls Selection
The control hardware was selected based on recommendations from Johns Hopkins professors
conducting research in the marine robotics sector, Baltimore-based maritime companies, ArduPilot
documentation, and community forums. The flight controller was the most critical component, as the
rest of the control system was designed around it. We selected the Pixhawk 6C due to its low cost,
compatibility with a variety of navigation software, high processing speed, and modular design. To
ensure seamless integration, we also purchased a power module from the same vendor to ensure
safe power delivery to the Pixhawk.

Figure 1.1: Pixhawk 6C Flight Controller
For positioning, we selected an M10 GPS and a DroneCAN F9P module, both recommended
by the Pixhawk documentation and known to provide high GPS accuracy when used together. We
reused an existing TF8B controller from previous years and purchased a compatible RC receiver to
avoid the cost of a new transmitter. Finally, we added a telemetry radio rated for up to 3 km range to
enable reliable communication with the ground station. After testing, the GNC system is capable of
centimeter-level accuracy and 0.75-mile communication range, which is well above what we expect
to encounter during the range.

1.4 Hull Trade Study
Based on our literature reviews, we were deciding between a multi- versus monohull craft. The
main advantage of a catamaran design is the reduced risk of rolling. However, the increased wetted
surface area (WSA) of a catamaran results in a greater thrust requirement at a given speed (see
Section 6.6). Given the course is just 4 loops around two buoys spaced 0.5 miles apart, we did not
find the catamaran’s advantages to be worth the increased required power.

with attached propellers, propeller ducts, and connection cables for controls, decreasing mechanical

pages.text:
are far too heavy, provide poor power delivery under high load, and suffer from severe voltage sag,
making them impractical for our needs. LiFePO₄ batteries provide a great overall balance: they offer
strong power output, stable voltage curves, significantly lower weight than lead-acid, and exceptional
cycle life. Furthermore, they are widely used in projects like ours and have extensive documentation
for implementation in marine environments. Due to this reason, we initially chose LiFePO₄ batteries
for the vessel, however, we ended up shifting gears towards LiPo due to LiFePO4 having a much
higher form factor and weight, significantly affecting the performance of our vessel. We didn’t choose
LiPo’s initially due to their high volatility and fast voltage drops. However, after creating physical and
digital fail safes, we feel comfortable using LiPo’s as our power source.

2. Design & Analysis

2.1 System Requirements
Most system requirements come from the PEP competition rules. Some additional
requirements were added by faculty members for logistical reasons. These are the main ones that
guided our design
Table 2.1 Abbreviated requirements
Requirements – The craft shall:
Be capable of transit in bay conditions (Sea State 2, Beaufort 3)
Fit in the bed of a standard bed pickup truck
Be watertight to IP67 standard
Be remote controlled, even if autonomous
Have a total voltage at or below 55.5 Volts and a total capacity below 500 Ah
Maximum speed of at least 15 knots
Have a main power disconnect and fuse through which all current must travel
Travel 2 miles and complete the race
Carry a 30-pound removable payload
Have a kill-switch that is engaged with navigation data is missing or corrupted

2.2 Propulsion
After looking at past PEP competitors and consulting professionals, we settled upon differential
thrust to steer our vessel, as opposed to an outboard motor and a rudder. While differential thrust
does cause a relatively significant drop in speed when turning, it overcomes a lot of challenges we
identified with having an outboard motor and rudder. Specifically, controlling a rudder with a servo
complicates our control system by requiring the system to have a more precise understanding of its
immediate environment. While having a rudder would be preferrable in a crewed or remotecontrolled vessel, having differential steering simplifies vessel dynamics to allow for more simple
autonomous control. Industry research revealed that USV’s with differential thrust can be modelled
as ground rovers, giving us a more intuitive understanding on how to calculate and manipulate
steering and turning dynamics in our control system
To size our propulsion system we chose an analytical solution over a computational
approach to allow for more rapid iteration. We used a method for v-shaped hulls found in The

a greater amount of load as opposed to the indoor test, raising our maximum current draw to 80 A as

maximum of 100A, reinsuring the safety of our circuitry.

2.5 Controls
While most of the components for the control system were selected to be inserted without
manufacturing, a significant effort was made to solder and extend the wires for our GPS, telemetry,
RC, and PWM output modules. Extending our cables served a variety of purposes, of which the
primary purpose was to allow us to best place our GPS and telemetry modules so that they have
improved accuracy and range.
The majority of our design in controls occurred on the software side in the form of tuning and
path planning. Despite being a work in progress, our autopilot software takes in the physical
limitations of the vessel, such as turning radius, maximum acceleration, and maximum speed, and
uses them to optimize performance. Aside from entering physical capabilities, tuning consists of
tuning PID and feed forward parameters for two main loops, Steering Rate and Speed Throttle.

Figure. 2.5 - ArduPilot Tuning Menu
The above figure shows some of the many tuning parameters that need to be entered to
optimize system performance. Aside from tuning, path planning consists of selecting waypoints for
the vessel to follow during the race. Key considerations when designing a path consist of
determining the number of waypoints on the path, waypoint radius, turning rate, and the speed and
at which the vessel chases the waypoints.
After meeting with engineers at Textron Systems in Hunt Valley, MD; we were introduced to the
Dubins path, which is the shortest trajectory between two points with specific starting and ending
orientations. Throughout the race we plan to model our path to be as similar as possible to a Dubins
path while staying within our physical limitations. If provided with enough time, we plan to use the
physical limitations of our vessel and run a variety of simulations using optimization algorithms to
determine the optimal path.

pages.text:
Figure 3.1: Full motor mount assembly (left); One motor mount with bracket removed (right)
The thrusters extend from the transom, positioning the propellers at least 3 inches below the
waterline, consistent with similar craft. The mounts, made from 1” aluminum tubing, were cut on a
bandsaw and drilled for fasteners, then connected using fabricated sheet metal brackets. Each
assembly was secured with ¼-20 stainless steel bolts and locknuts to resist vibration, and all
transom penetrations were sealed with silicone.

3.2 Frame
The PVC frame was cut to length using a PVC cutter and assembled using PVC cement (cold
welding). Openings in the forward section of the hull were created with a hole saw to allow the frame
members to pass through. These penetrations were sealed and secured using Sikaflex to ensure
waterproofing. A sheet metal stiffener plate was installed on the interior side to reinforce the
connection. Additionally, a PVC collar was heated and formed around the pipe to secure the panel
and improve load distribution.

3.3 Pontoons
The pontoons were designed to be simple extrusions that could be cut from foam rollers on a
bandsaw. A template was made using measurements from the pontoon analysis. This template was
then glued to the ends of foam rollers, which guided the bandsaw cuts. The hole in the middle is for
a PVC pipe insert. These PVC inserts connect to the frame described in Section 4.3. This system
was tested by placing 45 lbs of dead weight in the boat. 30 lbs were allocated for the payload, and
15 lbs were allocated for batteries and controls.

3.4 Lid
In accordance with waterproof requirements set by the competition, the hull had to be
completely sealed while in operation to protect onboard electronic components and prevent water
intake, both of which would severely inhibit performance or disqualify us from the race. As previously
discussed, the hull is made of fiberglass with a wooden back support and plastic top. To achieve full
waterproofing of the boat, this large entry point in the plastic top had to be covered and sealed while
not being a permanent solution to allow for easy access to internal components.

Figure 3.4: Waterproof lid with compression points; GPS, telemetry, and motor cable access
This was achieved through manufacturing a lid made from a waterproof box previously used for
testing cut to fit the contour of the top hole. The lid is made of solid black plastic that did not allow
any water passthrough, so the main point of interest was the interface between the lid and the hull.
To mitigate this, attachments points were made to attach the lid to the hull with bolts via small ¼-20
bolts. A total of 8 bolt-down points were added to the lid to provide close to uniform pressure across
the entire surface. This added pressure was used to compress a gasket lining on the lip of the hull,
which provided a watertight seal that protected internal electronics while also being able to be easily
removed for maintenance. Additional holes were drilled in the lid to provide air access to the GPS
transmitters and telemetry antenna. Cable glands were embedded into the lid to provide entry points
for motor cable connections to our control system. As a final defense layer, a layer of quick dry
silicone and waterproof tape can be added along the seam to ensure a watertight fit. This solution

3.5 Electronics
As most of the electronics were purchased and used as is, most of the building and fabricating
for controls consisted of securing electronics against vibrations, high temperature, and salt water.
This first consisted of connecting all our LiPo’s to heavy duty bus bars capable of handling up to
150A of current. These bus bars were fastened to the hull, while the batteries were adhered to the
hull via mounting tape. From there, all our wires were insulated with heat shrink and secured to the
hull using zip ties to minimize the effect of vibrations.
Additionally, all our electronics were temperature tested before being secured onto the vessel.
We identified the points of our circuit most vulnerable to high temperature to be our XT-60
connectors as they’re rated for 60 Amps continuous and 180 Amps peak. This is usually with 12
AWG wires, however, and we are using 10 AWG throughout our circuit, raising our maximum
current. To ensure our safety against high current, we ran 65 A throughout our circuit, in an enclosed
environment all while regularly measuring the temperature of the connectors. The figure below
shows that our connectors are more than capable of handling their expected load.
